title: Meeting Rooms II
description:
You are given a list of meeting time intervals `[start, end]`. Return the **minimum number of conference rooms** needed so that no two meetings share a room while they overlap.

A meeting that starts exactly when another ends may reuse that room.

examples.explanation: [0,30] occupies one room the whole time; [5,10] and [15,20] can share a second room.
All four are running at time 5.

hints: The answer is the maximum number of meetings that are in progress at the same instant.

Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of meetings currently using a room. When a new meeting starts, if the earliest-ending meeting has already finished, pop it (reuse the room). Push the new end. The heap size at its largest is the answer.
Alternative: sort starts and ends separately and sweep with two pointers, incrementing on a start and decrementing on an end (process an end first when it equals a start).
approach:
**Key insight: the number of rooms needed equals the maximum number of meetings overlapping at any single moment. Processing meetings by start time with a min-heap of end times tracks exactly that.**

Sort by start. The heap holds the end times of meetings that currently hold a room; its minimum is the room that frees up first. For each meeting, if that earliest end is `<= start`, the room is free and we replace its end time with ours; otherwise every room is busy and we push a new end. The largest heap size seen is the answer.

**Why it is correct:** at the moment a meeting starts, the heap contains precisely the meetings that started earlier and have not yet ended (plus possibly some that ended but were not popped because a free room was not needed; they only make the heap larger than necessary at that instant, and the maximum is still attained at some start time where all expired entries are reused first). Reusing the earliest-freed room never hurts because any free room is interchangeable.

**Alternative: two sorted arrays.** Sort starts and ends separately. Sweep: at each start, if the smallest unmatched end is `<= start`, a meeting finished and a room is released (advance the end pointer); otherwise allocate a room. This is the same idea without a heap and is a nice thing to mention.

**Common mistakes:** using `<` instead of `<=` for room reuse (back-to-back meetings should share a room); popping only one finished meeting per start is correct for the maximum, but students sometimes pop all and then compute size incorrectly; returning the final heap size instead of its maximum.

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) Which room does each meeting get (Meeting Rooms III: assign the lowest-indexed free room). (2) Report the time interval during which the most rooms are in use. (3) Rooms have capacities or meetings have attendee counts (sweep line with weights).
